title: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. (1983)
shortTitle: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. (1983)
summary: Rescinding a safety rule requires a reasoned explanation that addresses important alternatives and the available evidence.
notes: Justice White wrote for a unanimous Court on the standard of review, but Justice Rehnquist, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justices Powell and O'Connor, concurred in part and dissented in part, arguing that NHTSA had adequately explained rescinding the detachable automatic-belt requirement and that a new administration may legitimately reassess regulatory priorities.

sections.Parties: State Farm and an association of independent insurers challenged the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s rescission of a passive-restraint requirement. The Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association supported the rescission and sought Supreme Court review after the insurers prevailed below.
sections.Material Facts: The agency adopted a rule allowing manufacturers to satisfy passive crash-protection requirements through airbags or automatic belts. It initially expected substantial use of airbags, but manufacturers later planned to use detachable automatic belts in almost all cars. NHTSA rescinded the requirement in 1981 because it doubted those belts would increase use enough to justify implementation costs. It feared motorists would disconnect them and that expensive, ineffective equipment would discredit safety regulation. The agency did not reassess an airbags-only requirement or adequately explain rejection of continuous belts that could allow emergency exit without ordinary detachment.
sections.Procedural History: After reopening rulemaking, receiving comments, and holding hearings, NHTSA issued the rescission. The insurers petitioned for review, and the D.C. Circuit held the rescission arbitrary and capricious. The Supreme Court agreed that the explanation was inadequate but did not adopt all of the court of appeals’ reasoning. It vacated that court’s judgment and directed a remand to NHTSA for further consideration.
sections.Issue: What explanation does arbitrary-and-capricious review require when an agency rescinds an existing rule, and did NHTSA adequately justify abandoning passive-restraint requirements?
sections.Holding: Rescission receives the same arbitrary-and-capricious review as adoption. NHTSA failed to supply the required reasoned analysis, particularly by ignoring airbags as an alternative and inadequately treating automatic-belt evidence. The Court required agency reconsideration; it did not itself order adoption of a particular restraint technology.
sections.Reasoning: The Safety Act expressly subjected revocation to review, and reversal of an established policy required an explanation of the change. Doubts about detachable belts did not explain abandoning airbags, whose effectiveness the agency continued to accept. Lawyers’ later arguments could not supply reasons the agency itself had never given. The duty to consider alternatives did not extend to every imaginable option, but airbags were already central to the existing rule. The majority also required attention to inertia: once reconnected, an automatic belt continues to operate without another affirmative act, unlike a manual belt. Uncertainty can justify regulatory judgment, but the agency must explain what the evidence supports and how that bears on its choice. Rehnquist, joined by Burger, Powell, and O’Connor, agreed that omitted alternatives required explanation but would have sustained the agency’s detachable-belt assessment. He regarded an election and changed administrative priorities as a permissible basis for reassessment within statutory bounds. The excerpt distinguishes permissible changes in policy from an unexplained abandonment of a statutory task.

topics.lrs-n-hard-look: State Farm requires consideration of important existing alternatives and an explanation connecting the evidence to rescission.
topics.lrs-n-policy-change-reliance: Rescinding an existing safety standard required reasons addressing the retained technological alternatives and earlier judgments.
topics.lrs-n-administrative-record: Appellate counsel could not supply the airbag reasons that the agency itself had never given when rescinding the rule.
topics.lrs-o-chenery-reasons: The Court judged the rescission on the reasons NHTSA gave and refused to accept post hoc rationalizations by counsel.
